aiPlanner.metaDescription: Motir AI Planner asks until it is clear what you are building, then drafts the whole plan: every piece of work, in order, with who does it. Nothing starts until you approve it.
aiPlanner.headline: First the what. Then the whole plan.
aiPlanner.lede: Describe what you want to build. The planner asks until it is clear what you mean, because it won't plan a guess. Then it reads what already exists and drafts the whole plan: every piece of work, in the order it has to happen, with who does it. Nothing starts until you approve it.

steps.headline: It thinks it through with you

items.title: Asks until it's clear
items.body: If it isn't yet clear what you're building, it asks. It won't plan until it knows.

items.title: Reads what exists
items.body: Your repositories, documents and board, or a project you bring from Jira, Linear or Plane. It plans from where you are, not from a blank page.

items.title: Drafts the whole plan
items.body: Every piece of work from the big goals down to the small steps, each with who does it and what it waits on.

items.title: Checks its own work
items.body: Every plan is checked before you see it, so what reaches you is a plan that can be built.

gate.headline: You approve the plan
gate.body: Nothing reaches the board until you say so. Ask for changes in plain words: move this later, split that, drop the export. Each round is a new turn, and the plan keeps every version and the reason it changed.

items.title: The whole tree
items.body: Epics, stories, tasks and subtasks, from the goal down to the step.

items.title: Who does it
items.body: Each work item goes to an agent or to a person. Work only a person can do is a manual task.

items.title: The order
items.body: What waits on what, so each piece starts the moment it can.

items.title: The difficulty
items.body: A level on every work item, so it runs on a model that fits it.

items.title: The kind of work
items.body: Code, design, tests, documents, research, review: each kind is marked.

items.title: The schedule
items.body: Once you approve: sprints, a backlog and a roadmap.

learns.headline: It learns from every mistake
learns.body: When an agent can't build what the plan asked for, Motir first checks whether the plan was wrong or was changed after you approved it. A real planning mistake becomes a lesson, or strengthens one. Every new plan reads the lessons first, and a lesson that hasn't been needed for 90 days retires.
lessons: Put sign-in before anything that needs a user
Keep an email provider choice a manual task
Split a story that needs two kinds of work
Plan the empty state with the screen

board.headline: A board that knows what agents do
board.body: An agent's work moves through the same columns as everyone else's, with two that tell the truth about it. Implemented means an agent opened a pull request that nobody has checked yet. Approved means a person said yes and it hasn't shipped. Failing checks show on the work item itself.

aiDebugging.metaDescription: Bugs from production, from your team and from agents mid-run arrive traced to the code and planned. Motir AI names the likely cause, checks for a card that covers it, and resolves the Sentry error when the bug is done.
aiDebugging.headline: Every bug arrives traced to the code and planned.
aiDebugging.lede: From production, from someone on your team, or from an agent in the middle of a run: each bug lands with what done looks like, where in the code to start and what might be wrong. You decide who fixes it.

plan.headline: Possible causes, never a guess passed off as the answer
plan.body: The planner reads the stack trace against your repositories and writes the bug like a teammate would: what done looks like, where in the code to start, and why it matters. Likely causes are listed as possibilities to rule in or out, and when the trace can't be matched to your code, the bug says so.

fix.headline: Fix it by hand, or hand it to an agent
fix.body: A planned bug is an ordinary work item. Fix it yourself, or let an agent pick up the Bugs folder and open a pull request for each one. You review and merge, the bug is done, and the error is resolved in Sentry.

setup.headline: Connect once, choose what counts
setup.body: Connect your Sentry organization, then choose which of its projects send errors to this board. For each one, set the lowest level that counts, and whether finishing a bug resolves the error and whether Sentry's assignee carries over.

sources.headline: Three ways in, one kind of bug

items.title: Describe it to Motir AI
items.body: Tell it what's broken. It reads the code, names the likely cause, checks whether a card already covers it, then writes exactly one: a new bug or a note on the existing one.

items.title: From production
items.body: Connect Sentry and each new error becomes a bug with its stack trace. When it happens again, the count goes up, not the pile.

items.title: From an agent run
items.body: An agent that finds a bug outside its own work files it, with what it saw and where, and keeps going.

describe.headline: Say what's broken. Motir AI traces it.
describe.body: Describe the bug in your own words, or report it and hand it over. Motir AI reads your code and your plan, names the likely cause, and checks for a card that already covers it. It writes one thing and says exactly what: a new bug in Triage with the diagnosis, or the diagnosis added to the card that already tracks it. If it can't trace the bug to the code, it writes nothing.

production.headline: Errors arrive as bugs, with the evidence
production.body: Each new Sentry error becomes one bug work item with its exception, stack trace and a link back. When the bug is done, Motir resolves the error in Sentry. If it comes back, a new bug is filed, linked to the old one.

runs.headline: Agents report what they find
runs.body: An agent building one work item that hits a bug somewhere else doesn't stop and doesn't hide it. It files the bug with what it saw, notes the run it was found in, and carries on with its own work. The run lists every bug it filed.

agentFleet.metaDescription: Motir's hosted agents work every ready item of your plan at once, each on its own machine with a model that fits the job. Start them yourself or let Motir Project Manager keep them busy.
agentFleet.headline: Your whole plan, worked in parallel.
agentFleet.lede: Motir's hosted agents take every work item that is ready and work them at the same time, each on a fresh machine with its own branch and pull request. Start them yourself, or let Motir Project Manager keep them busy, and the project moves on every front at once.

parallel.headline: One machine for every ready work item
parallel.body: Everything that can start, starts. Each run claims its work item, so no two agents ever take the same one, and works it on a machine of its own. A story runs its pieces in the order they depend on each other. The more work is ready, the more runs at once.

pm.headline: Motir Project Manager keeps the fleet busy
pm.body: Hand the project to Motir Project Manager and it starts a run the moment a work item is ready, picks the model, and brings you only what needs your decision: the pull requests, the designs, the plans.

models.eyebrow: The right model for each job
models.headline: Every work item has a difficulty. It picks the model.
models.body: The planner gives every task, subtask and bug a difficulty: how hard the work is to get right, not how big it is. A one-line change to lock ordering can be high while a large rename is trivial. The fleet reads it to choose the model, so a rename doesn't pay for the strongest model and a data migration never runs on the cheapest.

items.title: Trivial
items.body: Mechanical work with an unambiguous spec: a rename, a copy change, a config flip. Runs on a faster, cheaper model.

items.title: Low
items.body: Routine work that follows a pattern the code already has, like a new field through an existing form. Runs on a faster, cheaper model.

items.title: Medium
items.body: Real design choices across several files or services, or a bug whose cause isn't known yet. Runs on the strongest model.

items.title: High
items.body: Work where a subtle mistake is costly: concurrency, security, a migration on live data. Runs on the strongest model.

items.title: Your choice
items.body: Set your own model for any level in the project, or pick one for a single run, from Claude, DeepSeek, GLM and Qwen.

items.title: Pay for what runs
items.body: Billed in credits for model calls and machine time. Nothing runs, nothing is billed.

models.docsLink: How difficulty levels work, and what a task costs on each model

items.title: Checks failing
items.body: A run repairs its pull request on the same branch, up to five attempts.

items.title: A run that died
items.body: The work stays on its branch, and a new run continues it without starting over.

items.title: A stalled agent
items.body: A run that goes quiet for 15 minutes is stopped, so a stuck agent never burns credits.

items.title: A bug along the way
items.body: An agent that finds a bug outside its own work files it and keeps going.

record.headline: Every run, step by step
record.body: Each run records its model, every step, what it cost and how each work item ended: implemented, failed, re-planned or skipped.

agentHosting.metaDescription: Run Claude Code, Codex or the agent you already use on its own machine in Motir's cloud, signed in with your own account. Send it work from Motir; it sleeps when you're done and you pay only for its machine time.
agentHosting.headline: Your own agents, on Motir's machines.
agentHosting.lede: Run Claude Code, Codex or the agent you already use in Motir's cloud, signed in with your own account and set up with your project's code. Send it a work item and close your laptop: it keeps working, and sleeps when you're done.

setup.headline: Three steps to your agent in the cloud

items.title: Create it
items.body: Name it, pick the project and the agent: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Aider or Goose. Your project's repositories are cloned into its home.

items.title: Sign in as you
items.body: Sign in from its terminal with your own account, the same way you would on your laptop.

items.title: Send it work
items.body: Press Send to my agent on any ready work item. It claims it, builds it on its own branch and opens a pull request.

away.headline: It keeps going when you close the laptop

items.title: Its own machine
items.body: Nothing runs on your laptop, so a closed lid or a dropped connection doesn't stop the work.

items.title: Watch from anywhere
items.body: Its runs show in Runs beside every other agent's, and its terminal is a click away in My agents.

items.title: Several at once
items.body: Keep up to ten agents, each working its own work item.

ui.title: My agents
ui.subtitle: Your own agents, on your own sign-in, in Motir's cloud — AI personal assistant

close.headline: Give your agent a desk.
close.body: Bring the agent you use, and let it work while you don't.

terms.headline: You pay for the machine, and only while it works

items.title: Your account, your model
items.body: The agent runs on your own sign-in, with the model and settings you chose. Its model usage is billed to you by its vendor, and Motir never sees your sign-in.

items.title: One credit a minute
items.body: Motir charges only the agent's machine time, one credit a minute while it runs.

items.title: Sleeps when you're done
items.body: After 30 minutes without use it hibernates and costs nothing but a little storage. It wakes when you send it the next work item.

howItWorks.lede: Every Motir project runs through the same instrument. The modules are Motir and its agents. The knobs and switches are yours: nothing moves forward until a person turns them.
howItWorks.rackTitle: The Motir workflow as a rack of modules
howItWorks.rackDesc: Your idea is patched into the planner, then into a knob where you approve the plan, then the board, then an agent run, then a knob where you review and merge, then Done. Manual tasks go from the board to Done. An agent run can log a bug it finds into the Bugs folder and keep going. A repair module loops failed runs back into the agent run. A learning loop runs from the agent run through a verdict, a re-plan and the lesson library back into the planner. A memory bank along the bottom holds designs, decisions, docs, lessons, run history, revisions and who decided what.

rack.engineSub: Blue modules do the work. Orange controls are yours.

howItWorks.modulesLede: Each module in the drawing above, up close. Hover one to find it in the drawing.

modules.label: [01] AI planning
modules.title: From a prompt to a plan
paras: Start with a sentence, a repository, or an import from Jira, Linear or Plane. The planner reads what exists, including a code graph of your repositories, and asks follow-up questions where the request is ambiguous.
It drafts epics, stories, tasks and subtasks, each with a type, an executor, a size and its `blocked_by` edges. `validate_plan` checks the tree before you see it.

modules.label: [02] You · plan gate
modules.title: You approve the plan
paras: Nothing lands on the board until a person approves the plan. Ask for changes in plain words; each round is a new turn, and the plan's history keeps every version and why it changed.

modules.label: [03] Work items
modules.title: The board
paras: The approved plan becomes work items with sprints, a backlog and a roadmap. Each work item's executor is `agent` or `human`.
Manual tasks (an account, a secret, a DNS record, a release sign-off) are walked through one step at a time by `motir guide`.

modules.label: [04] Agent run
modules.title: Agents build
paras: An agent takes the next ready work item (`motir next` or `motir run <KEY>`), claims it, builds on its own branch and opens one pull request per repository, linked to the work item.
A bug it finds outside its own work item doesn't stop the run: the agent root-causes it, files it with `motir log bug` into the Bugs folder as a work item of its own, and keeps going.
Each run records the agent harness, the model, every step and the outcome. Agents connect over MCP, on your machine or Motir's hosted agents.

modules.label: [05] You · merge gate
modules.title: You review and merge
paras: The work item moves to `Implemented` and the agent publishes How to test. Stories get an acceptance video recorded in CI. You review, approve and merge; the merge closes the work item. Nothing reaches `Done` without a person.

modules.label: [06] Repair
modules.title: When runs break
paras: A red or conflicting pull request is repaired on its own branch with `motir fix`, up to five attempts. A run that died (a laptop closed, a sandbox lost) is resumed with `motir continue` on the branch it left.
Bugs logged along the way wait in the Bugs folder; `motir fix bugs` works through them, oldest first.

modules.label: [07] Learning loop
modules.title: The planner learns
paras: An agent that can't build a work item first asks whether it is still what the approved plan approved (`get_approved_shape_verdict`), so a later edit isn't blamed on the planner. If the plan was wrong, it is re-planned and the change is recorded with its reason.
The mistake becomes a lesson, or reinforces one; with no rule to cover it, a planning bug is filed. The next plan reads the lessons first. Lessons that don't recur for 90 days retire.

modules.label: [08] Memory
modules.title: The project remembers
paras: Designs, decision pages, docs, lessons, plan revisions and every run's history live next to the work items. You, a new teammate or the next agent can pick the project up months later without anyone explaining it again.

ideas.metaDescription: Products Motir would buy: AI platforms for the work a software company can't do with code alone. Build one that scales, and Motir will be your first customer.
ideas.headline: Build what Motir would buy.
ideas.lede: A software company runs on more than code. It needs a lawyer, an accountant, a security team and people who know other markets, and Motir is no different. We would rather buy that work from a product built on Motir. These are the ones we need. Build one that scales, and Motir will be your first customer.
ideas.promiseBody: Build one of these on Motir, in public, and we will use it, pay for it and tell you what is missing.
ideas.rulesEyebrow: What makes a good idea here
ideas.rulesHeadline: Products that scale, not tools for one team

rules.title: Many customers, one product
rules.body: Every idea serves thousands of companies with the same problem, not one company's own process.

rules.title: Expertise you can't hire cheaply
rules.body: Law, tax, security, languages: work that needs a specialist, made affordable by AI and kept honest by people.

rules.title: A person still signs
rules.body: The AI drafts, checks and files the work. A qualified person approves what carries risk, the same way Motir puts a person at every gate.

ideas.listHeadline: Six products Motir would buy today

items.title: An AI legal team for software companies
items.pitch: Terms, privacy policies, data processing agreements and the record of every vendor that touches customer data, drafted, kept current and reviewed by a lawyer.
does: Drafts and updates terms, privacy policies and data processing agreements as the product changes
Reviews vendor and customer contracts and flags what needs a lawyer
Tracks new rules, like the EU AI Act, and says what each one changes for you
items.need: Every model provider Motir adds needs a data processing agreement and a recorded legal basis for sending customer data to it. Today that is slow, manual work.
items.who: Every software company that handles customer data, which is all of them.

items.title: An AI finance team for startups
items.pitch: Price the plans, bill for usage, file the taxes and pay the vendors, from one place that understands what each customer actually costs.
does: Sets plan prices from real costs: model calls, machine time, storage
Reconciles usage billing and files sales tax and VAT in every country you sell to
Pays vendors, tracks runway and closes the books each month
items.need: Motir resells model calls and machine minutes at a margin. Pricing a plan means knowing the cost of every credit, in every currency, after tax.
items.who: Every usage-priced software startup, from its first invoice to its first audit.

items.title: AI security and compliance, from the evidence
items.pitch: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence collected from the code, the cloud and the project itself, and security questionnaires answered from it.
does: Collects evidence from repositories, cloud accounts and the project's history
Answers customer security questionnaires from that evidence, with sources
Watches for drift and opens a work item when a control slips
items.need: A business customer asks for a security review before it signs. Every answer is somewhere in Motir's code and records, and finding it takes days we would rather spend building.
items.who: Every software company selling to a business big enough to ask.

items.title: AI support that knows the product
items.pitch: Answers customers from the docs, the code and the live state of the product, and turns a real bug into a planned work item instead of a reply.
does: Answers from documentation, code and the customer's own account
Hands a real defect to the engineering team as a planned work item, with the evidence
Learns from every answer a person corrects
items.need: Motir's users ask about agents, models, credits and repositories. A good answer needs the code and the account, not a help-center search.
items.who: Every developer-tool and B2B software company with more customers than support staff.

items.title: AI localization that keeps up with the product
items.pitch: Translates the interface, the docs and the emails as they change, keeps every term consistent, and has a native speaker review what matters.
does: Translates each change as it lands, not in a yearly project
Keeps a glossary so a term means one thing everywhere
Sends the risky strings, legal text and pricing to a native reviewer
items.need: Motir ships in English and Chinese, and every release changes hundreds of strings. Keeping both right by hand does not scale to a third language.
items.who: Every software company that wants customers outside its home country.

items.title: AI growth for B2B software
items.pitch: Turns what a team ships into launch posts, changelog announcements, comparison pages and search-ready docs, and measures what brings customers.
does: Writes the announcement for each release from the work that shipped
Builds and refreshes the pages people search for before they buy
Shows which pages and posts bring customers, not just visitors
items.need: Motir ships every day, in public. Turning that into posts and pages people find takes a marketing team we do not have.
items.who: Every B2B software company that ships faster than it can tell anyone.

close.headline: Build one. We'll be your first customer.
close.body: Start with the idea, plan it with Motir and build it in public. Pick one of these, or bring your own.

ideas.placeholder: An AI finance team for startups: it prices the plans, files sales tax and pays the vendors…

more.headline: Good products to build, beyond what Motir needs
more.body: Motir won't be your first customer for these. Each is a market with documented demand, a gap the current players leave open, and a reason it can be built now and not five years ago. The evidence is linked under each one.

ideas.title: Make a store visible to AI shoppers
ideas.pitch: Gets a small store's products found and recommended by the AI assistants people now shop through, and shows how often each product is picked.
ideas.evidence: Traffic from AI assistants to US retail sites rose 693% in the 2025 holiday season and converted 31% better than other traffic.
ideas.sourceName: Adobe Analytics, via Digital Commerce 360, January 2026
ideas.gap: The funded players sell to large brands and big catalogs. Millions of small stores have nothing yet, and the window is short.

ideas.title: Stop returns before they happen
ideas.pitch: Spots the order bought in three sizes to send two back, answers the fit question before checkout, and scores each return for fraud.
ideas.evidence: Shoppers were expected to return $849.9 billion of goods in 2025, 19.3% of online sales, and 9% of returns are fraudulent.
ideas.sourceName: National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, October 2025
ideas.gap: Return platforms handle the return once it starts. Preventing it, for stores below enterprise size, is barely served.

ideas.title: APIs that update their customers' code
ideas.pitch: When an API makes a breaking change, the provider opens the pull request that migrates each customer's code, instead of sending an email.
ideas.evidence: On Y Combinator's Fall 2026 Requests for Startups: API providers shouldn't just announce changes; they should apply them.
ideas.sourceName: Y Combinator, Requests for Startups, Fall 2026
ideas.gap: Dependency bots only bump version numbers, and SDK generators don't touch customer code. Agents can now edit unfamiliar code well enough to open the pull request.

ideas.title: AI cost by feature and by customer
ideas.pitch: Splits the AI bill by feature and by customer, sets budgets, and shows finance and engineering the margin of every plan in one view.
ideas.evidence: 79% of finance leaders report AI cost overruns, and only 15% can calculate the return on AI spend without significant bottlenecks.
ideas.sourceName: DoiT and Sapio Research, survey of 500 finance leaders, February 2026
ideas.gap: Cloud cost tools are built around the cloud bill, and AI observability tools are built for developers. Neither gives finance a margin per feature.

ideas.title: The AI transparency kit
ideas.pitch: A drop-in kit that tells users they're talking to an AI, marks generated content in a machine-readable way and labels deepfakes, as the EU now requires.
ideas.evidence: The EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, with systems already on the market given until 2 December 2026, and fines of up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover.
ideas.sourceName: Jones Walker, AI Law Blog, July 2026
ideas.gap: Content-marking vendors serve enterprises or one platform. A small app maker has no simple way to comply before the deadline.

ideas.title: A first tutor for young children
ideas.pitch: A voice tutor at home that teaches four-to-eight-year-olds to read, write and count, one child at a time, at the child's own pace.
ideas.evidence: On Y Combinator's Fall 2026 Requests for Startups as "The Primer", noting the cost of the AI per child is falling about ten times a year.
ideas.sourceName: Y Combinator, Requests for Startups, Fall 2026
ideas.gap: Ello, the funded AI tutor for this age, teaches reading only, and the best-known AI tutors are built for schools, not homes.

ideas.title: A career coach for people who pay for themselves
ideas.pitch: Coaching and practice conversations for the job you want next, for the many workers whose employer won't pay for training.
ideas.evidence: Valence raised a $50 million Series B for AI coaching, after more than a million coaching conversations, showing AI coaching works when employers buy it.
ideas.gap: AI coaching is sold only to employers, and learning platforms sell courses, not coaching. Nobody serves the person who pays for themselves.

ideas.title: Treatment options for vet clinics
ideas.pitch: During the exam, turns one diagnosis into two or three priced treatment plans with a payment plan attached, so the pet gets care the owner can afford.
ideas.evidence: 94% of vets say cost stops recommended care, and 81% say they offer alternatives, yet 73% of pet owners say they were never offered a cheaper plan.
ideas.sourceName: Gallup and PetSmart Charities, survey of 933 vets, 2025
ideas.gap: Vet AI tools write the visit notes and practice software books the visits. None turns a case into priced options.

ideas.title: A care team app for families
ideas.pitch: Shares medicines, tasks and appointments across the family looking after a parent, and explains each care task in plain words.
ideas.evidence: 63 million Americans are family caregivers, about 45% more than in 2015. More than half do medical or nursing tasks, and only 20% have been trained.
ideas.sourceName: AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, July 2025
ideas.gap: Care coordination is sold to employers as a benefit, or comes with paid carers. The free apps families use are basic.

setupPrompt.title: Set up Motir in your agent
setupPrompt.body: Copy one prompt and paste it into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any other agent. It connects Motir's MCP server, installs the CLI and the skills, and checks they work. In Claude Code it installs the Motir plugin.

builtByMotirPage.headline: How Motir builds Motir.
builtByMotirPage.lede: It sounds like a chicken-and-egg problem. It isn't. Motir started as a folder of prompts, and every feature it shipped became a tool for building the next one.
builtByMotirPage.runs: Create an account to watch its agent runs

lost.headline: We vibe coded. The project fell apart.
lost.body: Vibe coding made the code fast. But the further we got, the more of the project we lost — because a project is not only code.

items.title: A bug found, never tracked
items.body: Spotted in the middle of a session, forgotten by the end of it.

items.title: Too much at once
items.body: Five features in flight, and no way to tell which one to start next.

items.title: Tests that weren't there
items.body: Missing, or not up to the standard the rest of the code needed.

items.title: Decisions lost in a chat
items.body: Why something was built that way ended when the coding session did.

missing.headline: Jira and Linear track work. We needed more.
missing.body: We plugged our process into the project tools we knew. They held the tasks, but not the thing we were missing.

items.title: A plan before the code
items.body: An agent should start from a plan a person approved, not from a prompt.

items.title: Ready, or blocked by what
items.body: See which work can start now, and which waits — on exactly which other work.

items.title: Someone running the whole project
items.body: A project manager that oversees everything and puts it together, without being asked.

bootstrap.headline: Every feature becomes the tool for the next.
bootstrap.body: Motir didn't wait to be finished before it was used. Each feature it shipped replaced the scaffolding it was built with.

steps.title: motir-meta
steps.body: An internal project: a set of prompts, a task list and a store of mistakes. It prompted a model to build Motir's first features.

steps.title: Work items
steps.body: With work items shipped, Motir asked itself what to build next, not an outside tool.

steps.title: The MCP server
steps.body: With the MCP shipped, those lookups became MCP calls, and status kept itself in sync.

steps.title: AI planning
steps.body: With planning shipped, Motir planned its next features with its own planner.

steps.title: Agents and approvals
steps.body: Agents build Motir's work items; a person approves every plan and every merge.

loop: Build the next one with it

live.headline: It hasn't stopped.
live.body: Motir is still adding features to itself, in public. These numbers are live from Motir's own project.

close.headline: Build yours the same way.
close.body: Start with an idea. Motir plans it, builds it and keeps the whole project together.
